data.body:
_Viva questions for the case: **Dermatomyositis** (Connective tissue diseases)_

**Q1. Define dermatomyositis (DM).**
- Idiopathic inflammatory myopathy with characteristic skin lesions and proximal symmetrical muscle weakness; part of the IIM group (with polymyositis, inclusion body myositis, immune-mediated necrotising myopathy, antisynthetase syndrome)
- Bimodal: juvenile (5–15 y) and adult (40–60 y), women 2:1

**Q2. Classify dermatomyositis (Bohan & Peter / Sontheimer).**
- Classic adult DM, juvenile DM, cancer-associated DM, DM overlapping with other CTD
- Clinically amyopathic DM (CADM): skin signs ≥6 months without weakness — amyopathic (normal muscle tests) and hypomyopathic (subclinical abnormal tests)
- Polymyositis (no skin), inclusion body myositis

**Q3. Describe the pathognomonic and characteristic skin signs (Gottron's — PYQ).**
- Pathognomonic: Gottron's papules (violaceous flat-topped papules over knuckles — MCP, PIP, DIP joints) and Gottron's sign (violaceous macules/patches over extensor surfaces of joints — elbows, knees, knuckles, malleoli)
- Characteristic: heliotrope rash (violet-purple erythema ± oedema of upper eyelids), periungual telangiectasia with cuticular overgrowth and haemorrhages (ragged cuticles — Samitz sign), poikiloderma of photo-exposed areas — V-sign (anterior neck/chest), shawl sign (back and shoulders), holster sign (lateral thighs)
- Others: scalp erythema with scaling and non-scarring alopecia, mechanic's hands (hyperkeratotic fissured lateral fingers — antisynthetase syndrome), calcinosis cutis (juvenile), flagellate erythema, Raynaud's, ulcers (MDA5), panniculitis, vasculitis, pruritus (more than in lupus — helps differentiate)

**Q4. Describe the muscle involvement.**
- Proximal symmetrical weakness of shoulder and hip girdles (difficulty combing hair, rising from squatting, climbing stairs), neck flexors, pharyngeal muscles (dysphagia, nasal regurgitation, aspiration), respiratory muscles; myalgia; distal and facial muscles spared

**Q5. Myositis-specific autoantibodies and their associations.**
- Anti-Mi-2: classic DM, prominent skin, good response, low cancer risk
- Anti-TIF1γ (p155/140): strong association with malignancy in adults; severe skin, 'red on white' lesions, palmar hyperkeratotic papules
- Anti-NXP2: calcinosis in juvenile DM, adult malignancy, oedema
- Anti-MDA5 (CADM-140): clinically amyopathic DM, rapidly progressive interstitial lung disease (high mortality — especially in Asians), palmar papules (inverse Gottron's), skin ulcers, arthritis
- Anti-SAE: skin first then muscle, dysphagia
- Antisynthetase (anti-Jo-1, PL-7, PL-12, EJ, OJ): myositis, ILD, mechanic's hands, arthritis, Raynaud's, fever

**Q6. How do you investigate DM?**
- Muscle enzymes: CK (most sensitive), aldolase, LDH, AST/ALT; may be normal in CADM
- EMG (myopathic pattern: short polyphasic potentials, fibrillation), MRI of thighs (oedema on STIR — guides biopsy), muscle biopsy (perifascicular atrophy, perivascular inflammation, MxA expression)
- Skin biopsy: interface dermatitis with dermal mucin (similar to lupus); DIF usually negative (unlike lupus)
- ANA, myositis-specific/associated antibody panel
- ILD screen: HRCT chest, PFTs (DLCO); ECG/echo for cardiac; barium swallow/manometry for dysphagia
- Cancer screening in adults (especially first 3 years): CBC, CT chest–abdomen–pelvis, ovarian (CA-125, pelvic USG), breast, colorectal, nasopharyngeal (in Asians), PSA; repeat annually for 3 years

**Q7. Which malignancies are associated with DM?**
- 15–25% of adult DM; ovarian, lung, breast, stomach, colorectal, pancreatic, nasopharyngeal carcinoma (Southeast Asia/China), lymphoma
- Risk factors: age >45–50, male, TIF1γ/NXP2 antibodies, rapid onset, cutaneous necrosis/ulcers, dysphagia, normal CK, poor treatment response

**Q8. Juvenile DM — differences from adult.**
- More vasculopathy (ulceration, lipodystrophy, GI vasculitis), calcinosis (up to 40%), no malignancy association, better prognosis; treat aggressively early (methotrexate + steroids) to prevent calcinosis

**Q9. Differentiate DM from SLE skin disease.**
- DM: violaceous, itchy, over knuckles (Gottron's), heliotrope, scalp involvement, shawl/V sign poikiloderma, periungual changes, muscle weakness, raised CK
- SLE: pink-red, less itchy, between knuckles (spares joints), malar rash spares nasolabial folds, photosensitivity, ANA/anti-dsDNA, DIF lupus band positive

**Q10. Management of DM.**
- Photoprotection (broad-spectrum sunscreen), physiotherapy, speech therapy for dysphagia
- Systemic corticosteroids prednisolone 1 mg/kg/day (or IV methylprednisolone pulse for severe) tapered over months
- Steroid-sparing from the start: methotrexate 15–25 mg/week, azathioprine, mycophenolate (also for ILD)
- Skin: topical steroids/tacrolimus, hydroxychloroquine (watch drug rash — common in DM), methotrexate, dapsone, IVIG (very effective for skin and muscle — approved for DM), JAK inhibitors (tofacitinib — refractory skin and MDA5-ILD)
- Refractory: IVIG, rituximab, cyclophosphamide/tacrolimus (ILD), cyclosporine
- Calcinosis: diltiazem, bisphosphonates, probenecid, sodium thiosulphate (topical/intralesional/IV), surgical excision
- Treat underlying malignancy (DM may remit)

**Q11. Prognosis.**
- 5-year survival ~70–90%; worse with malignancy, ILD (MDA5), dysphagia/aspiration, cardiac involvement, older age, delayed treatment

**Q12. Describe the less common skin signs of DM.**
- Mechanic's hands (antisynthetase), palmar papules and ulcers over joint creases (MDA5 — 'inverse Gottron's'), flagellate erythema (scratch-like linear erythema on back), 'V-neck', shawl, holster signs, scalp dermatomyositis (scaly itchy, mimics psoriasis/seb derm), poikiloderma, calcinosis, panniculitis, erythroderma, vesiculobullous DM (malignancy), ovoid palatal patch (TIF1γ), 'red on white' lesions, Wong-type DM (PRP-like follicular hyperkeratosis)

**Q13. What is the mechanism of photosensitivity and itch in DM?**
- UV-induced keratinocyte apoptosis increases autoantigen exposure (Mi-2, TIF1γ) and type I IFN production; itch is prominent (IL-31, IFN) — helps differentiate from lupus; photoprotection is essential

**Q14. Muscle biopsy findings.**
- Perifascicular atrophy (pathognomonic), perivascular and perimysial inflammation (CD4 T, B cells, plasmacytoid DCs), MxA overexpression in perifascicular fibres (type I IFN), capillary dropout with complement (MAC) deposition in capillaries
- Polymyositis — endomysial CD8 T-cell invasion; IMNM — necrotic fibres with little inflammation (anti-SRP, anti-HMGCR — statins)

**Q15. What is the antisynthetase syndrome?**
- Anti-aminoacyl tRNA synthetase antibodies (Jo-1 commonest, PL-7, PL-12, EJ, OJ, KS): myositis + ILD + non-erosive arthritis + mechanic's hands + Raynaud's + fever; ILD determines prognosis — treat with steroids + MMF/tacrolimus/ rituximab

**Q16. Clinically amyopathic DM — what is important?**
- Skin-predominant (≥6 months) with normal or subclinical muscle tests; still needs malignancy screening and ILD screening — especially anti-MDA5 (rapidly progressive ILD, high mortality in Asians: treat early with steroids + calcineurin inhibitor + cyclophosphamide/ JAK inhibitor; ferritin and KL-6 track severity)

**Q17. Calcinosis in juvenile DM — types and treatment.**
- Superficial plaques/ nodules, deep tumoral masses, intermuscular fascial plane calcification, exoskeleton-like (severe); can ulcerate and extrude chalky material
- Prevention: early aggressive immunosuppression (MTX + steroids, IVIG); treatment: diltiazem, bisphosphonates, sodium thiosulphate (IV/intralesional/topical), probenecid, colchicine, surgery for symptomatic deposits, JAK inhibitors (case series)

**Q18. How is DM disease activity measured?**
- CDASI (Cutaneous Dermatomyositis Disease Area and Severity Index — activity and damage), MMT-8 (manual muscle testing of 8 muscle groups), CK, HAQ, IMACS core set measures, total improvement score (ACR/EULAR 2016)

**Q19. Physiotherapy and rehabilitation role.**
- Early supervised exercise is safe and improves strength and function (even in active disease); prevents contractures; swallowing therapy for dysphagia; dietary advice, aspiration precautions

**Q20. Differential diagnosis of proximal weakness with rash.**
- SLE/MCTD overlap, hypothyroid myopathy, steroid myopathy, statin myopathy (anti-HMGCR), trichinosis, sarcoid myopathy, HIV myositis, muscular dystrophies (no rash), inclusion body myositis (distal/ quadriceps, finger flexors, older men, no rash)

**Q21. Describe heliotrope rash and its differentials.**
- Violaceous erythema ± oedema of upper eyelids (sometimes lower), may extend to periorbital skin; differentials — allergic contact dermatitis (eyelids), angioedema, SLE, trichinosis, nephrotic oedema, rosacea, atopic eyelid dermatitis, myxoedema

**Q22. What drugs can induce DM-like eruptions?**
- Hydroxyurea (DM-like on knuckles without myositis), statins, penicillamine, TNF inhibitors, checkpoint inhibitors, BCG vaccine, interferons, NSAIDs

**Q23. Discuss IVIG in DM.**
- 2 g/kg over 2–5 days monthly — proven (ProDERM trial) for skin and muscle; also refractory dysphagia, calcinosis prevention in JDM; side effects — headache, aseptic meningitis, thrombosis, renal failure (sucrose-containing), anaphylaxis in IgA deficiency; costly

**Q24. How do you monitor for malignancy over time?**
- Screen at diagnosis and annually for 3 years (risk highest in first 3 years); repeat CT chest/abdomen/pelvis ± PET-CT in high-risk (TIF1γ, NXP2, older age, dysphagia, cutaneous necrosis); gender-specific (mammography, Pap/ CA-125 and pelvic ultrasound, PSA), colonoscopy, nasopharyngoscopy in Southeast Asians

**Q25. What is the role of hydroxychloroquine in DM skin and its risk?**
- Useful for photosensitive skin lesions with sunscreen; but drug eruptions (morbilliform) occur much more often in DM than lupus (~30%, especially anti-SAE positive); quinacrine or methotrexate alternatives; monitor eyes

**Q26. Prognostic factors in DM.**
- Poor: malignancy, ILD (MDA5, antisynthetase), cardiac involvement, dysphagia/ aspiration pneumonia, older age, male sex, delayed treatment, high CK in adults with severe weakness; juvenile DM has good survival but calcinosis morbidity

**Q27. What are the overlap myositis antibodies?**
- Anti-PM/Scl (SSc–myositis overlap, mechanic's hands, calcinosis, ILD), anti-Ku (SLE/ SSc overlap), anti-U1RNP (MCTD), anti-Ro52 (with antisynthetase/ ILD — severe), anti-SRP and anti-HMGCR (necrotising myopathy)

**Q28. Pregnancy and DM.**
- Disease activity at conception predicts outcome; risks of fetal loss and prematurity with active disease; prednisolone, azathioprine, IVIG, HCQ, tacrolimus can be used; stop methotrexate/ MMF/ cyclophosphamide before conception

**Q29. Why is anti-TIF1γ important in children vs adults?**
- In juvenile DM it is the commonest antibody and is NOT linked to cancer (associated with severe skin disease, lipodystrophy and chronic course); in adults it strongly predicts malignancy (≈ 20–65%)

**Q30. Treatment of refractory skin disease in DM.**
- Methotrexate, MMF, IVIG, dapsone, JAK inhibitors (tofacitinib, ruxolitinib — strong efficacy on skin and MDA5-ILD), apremilast, lenalidomide/ thalidomide, rituximab (better for muscle), anifrolumab under trial; antihistamines/ gabapentin for itch

## Quick spotter facts
- Gottron's papules over knuckles + heliotrope eyelids — dermatomyositis
- Anti-MDA5 — rapidly progressive ILD; anti-TIF1γ — cancer
- Screen for malignancy in adults

_Sources: Previous-year PG question papers (Sahana P Raju, Solved Papers Dermatology); IADVL Textbook of Dermatology 5e (Dermatomyositis); 2017 EULAR/ACR idiopathic inflammatory myopathy criteria. Answers written in our own words; check with your teachers' preferences._
